questions.question: Tell me about a time something you built failed in front of real users, and what you did.

structure.evidence: During a live class, our Campus Attendance App started marking some students present twice.

relevance.evidence: During a live class, our Campus Attendance App started marking some students present twice.

depth.evidence: I moved marking into a Firestore transaction with a duplicate check, and added an idempotency key per student and session.

clarity.evidence: Duplicates dropped to zero over the next week, and I wrote a test that fires 20 parallel scans so it cannot come back unnoticed.

questions.good: Exemplary STAR response with clear technical diagnosis and quantitative proof of resolution.

questions.modelAnswer: While 400 students used the Campus Attendance App across six classes, duplicate records occurred when two scans happened within one second. I identified missing concurrency control, refactored backend writes to use Firestore transactions with idempotency keys per session, and added a automated test firing 20 parallel scans. This eliminated duplicate records completely while keeping live updates under 1 second.

questions.question: Since this is a payments company, how would you design an API so that a payment is never charged twice when the client retries?

structure.evidence: I would use an idempotency key.

relevance.evidence: The client sends a unique key with every payment request.

depth.evidence: The server stores that key together with the result of the first attempt, in the same database transaction as the charge.

clarity.evidence: If the same key arrives again, it returns the stored result instead of charging again.

questions.good: Delivered a clear and correct system design approach to idempotency in payment processing APIs.
questions.fix: Mention specific HTTP status codes and state machine transitions used for handling concurrent duplicate retries.
questions.modelAnswer: To prevent double charging, the API requires clients to submit a unique idempotency key per payment attempt. The server saves this key along with the charge result inside PostgreSQL within the same database transaction. Subsequent requests with the identical key return the stored response without re-executing the transaction, while invalid payload reuses are rejected.

questions.question: Your Library Seat Finder query got much faster. Walk me through how you found the bottleneck.

structure.evidence: I turned on slow query logging in Postgres and saw the seat map took about 900 milliseconds.

depth.evidence: It was a sequential scan over roughly 200,000 rows, because the only index was on seat id.

clarity.evidence: The query dropped to around 80 milliseconds.

questions.good: Demonstrated systematic database profiling methodology using standard tools like EXPLAIN ANALYZE.
questions.fix: Isolate and state the latency reduction contributed by the composite index versus the summary table.
questions.modelAnswer: While developing the Library Seat Finder using Python and PostgreSQL, the seat map load time reached 900 ms on 200,000 rows. Using EXPLAIN ANALYZE, I identified a sequential scan caused by indexing only the seat ID, then created a composite index on seat ID and timestamp alongside a latest-status summary table. This lowered query execution time to 80 ms, helping reduce overall seat searching time for students by 30%.
